explanations.answer: That none of them falls short of it
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The writer says, "Therefore, while the promise of entering His rest still stands, let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it." (Hebrews 4:1) Notice he says "let us." He puts himself right in there with the readers. Nobody gets left standing at the counter alone.

explanations.answer: That none of them shares it too soon
explanations.explanation: Ha, nobody in this passage is told to hold the good news back. The writer says to be careful that none of them be deemed to have fallen short of the rest (Hebrews 4:1). Sharing too soon is a worry I'd love to have, honestly. The real concern is falling short of the promise.

explanations.answer: That none of them argues about it
explanations.explanation: Arguing never comes up here, friend. The writer says, "…let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it." (Hebrews 4:1) The care is about falling short of the promised rest. Keep the arguments out of my bakery anyway, I have enough noise from the timer.

explanations.answer: They did not share the faith of those who understood it
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The writer says the message they heard was of no value to them, "since they did not share the faith of those who comprehended it." (Hebrews 4:2) They heard the same good news the readers did. The difference was faith. Hearing it wasn't enough.

explanations.answer: They heard it from someone they did not trust at all
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. It says the message was of no value to them "since they did not share the faith of those who comprehended it." (Hebrews 4:2) Nothing is said about who they heard it from or whether they trusted him. The problem was the faith that was missing.

explanations.answer: They heard it only once and soon forgot it
explanations.explanation: I've forgotten plenty in my day, like where I put my own mustache wax. But the writer doesn't blame forgetting here. He says they did not "share the faith of those who comprehended it." (Hebrews 4:2) The text says nothing about how many times they heard it.
Believed, that's it. The writer says, "Now we who have believed enter that rest." (Hebrews 4:3) It lines up with verse 2, where the others lacked faith. Simple, clear, and no secret recipe needed.
Waiting sounds right, since I did plenty of it in a drawer. But the writer says, "Now we who have believed enter that rest." (Hebrews 4:3) The word is believed. Waiting alone doesn't get anybody in.

Skipping meals isn't the word here, friend. The writer says, "Now we who have believed enter that rest." (Hebrews 4:3) Believing is what the verse names. Fasting isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage.

True, baker. The writer says, "For somewhere He has spoken about the seventh day in this manner: 'And on the seventh day God rested from all His works.'" (Hebrews 4:4) That goes all the way back to creation. It's the same line we find in Genesis 2:2.

Not false, friend. The writer says, "For somewhere He has spoken about the seventh day in this manner: 'And on the seventh day God rested from all His works.'" (Hebrews 4:4) So he really does point back to the seventh day. The text says God rested from all His works.
Yes, friend. God says through David, "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts." (Hebrews 4:7) Hearing His voice is the moment that matters. A hard heart is the thing to avoid.

Looking back at Egypt is a good guess with this crowd, but it isn't the line. David's words are, "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts." (Hebrews 4:7) The warning is about hearts, not about glancing over a shoulder.

No sign requests here, baker. The line is, "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts." (Hebrews 4:7) The warning is about hardening hearts. Asking for signs never comes up in this passage.

Careful, friend, this one is the opposite. The writer says, "For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day." (Hebrews 4:8) So Joshua didn't give them that rest. God kept talking about another day afterward.

You've got it, baker. The writer says, "For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day." (Hebrews 4:8) Joshua led Israel into the land, but God still spoke of another day later. So the rest the writer means wasn't already given.

Work, that's the word. The writer says, "For whoever enters God's rest also rests from his own work, just as God did from His." (Hebrews 4:10) The pattern is God's own rest. I'd say my rest is my own, but I stamp cookies all day, so I'm not one to talk.

Worry sounds like a nice thing to rest from, I'll give you that. But the verse says, "For whoever enters God's rest also rests from his own work, just as God did from His." (Hebrews 4:10) God rested from His works, so the matching word is work.

I understand why fear came to mind, friend. But the verse says whoever enters God's rest "also rests from his own work, just as God did from His." (Hebrews 4:10) The comparison is with God's works, so the word is work. Fear isn't what the verse names.

explanations.answer: So no one falls by following the same pattern of disobedience
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says, "Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one will fall by following the same pattern of disobedience." (Hebrews 4:11) The pattern he means is the one from the wilderness people. He wants nobody to fall the way they did.

explanations.answer: So they earn a greater reward than the others
explanations.explanation: No reward race here, friend. The writer says to make every effort "so that no one will fall by following the same pattern of disobedience." (Hebrews 4:11) The reason given is not falling. Beating the others isn't in the text.

explanations.answer: So God will see who works the very hardest
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. The effort is urged "so that no one will fall by following the same pattern of disobedience." (Hebrews 4:11) Nobody is being ranked. I'll admit I ranked my own cookies once, and even the burnt ones felt judged.

explanations.answer: The thoughts and intentions of the heart
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says the word of God "judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart." (Hebrews 4:12) It goes deep, all the way to soul and spirit, joints and marrow. Nothing in there stays out of reach.

explanations.answer: The deeds and records of the nations
explanations.explanation: Nations don't come up in this verse, friend. The word of God "judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart." (Hebrews 4:12) This is about what's inside a person. It's a lot closer to home than any record.

explanations.answer: The words and promises of the priests
explanations.explanation: Priests aren't named here, baker. The verse says the word of God "judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart." (Hebrews 4:12) That reaches every person's heart. It doesn't single out any one group.
True, friend. The writer says everything is uncovered and exposed "before the eyes of Him to whom we must give account." (Hebrews 4:13) The verse says it plainly. God is the One we give account to.

Not false, baker. The writer says everything is uncovered and exposed "before the eyes of Him to whom we must give account." (Hebrews 4:13) So the verse really does say we give account to God. I think that's a sober line, and the text says it plainly.
